VED en Gennemsøgning af det kongelige Biblioteks lægeviden-
skabelige Manuskripter, foretaget med Henblik paa, om muligt,
at forøge Kendskabet til de danske Læger i Middelalderen, traf jeg
i Manuskriptet G. k. S. 1654, 4° en Afhandling, De simplicibus medi-
cinis laxativis, skrevet af en hidtil ukendt Forfatter, Henricus Dacus
eller de Dacia. Det nævnte Manuskript er velkendt, ikke mindst
paa Grund af dets Indhold af en Macertekst, men Henricus Dacus'
Afhandling synes hidtil ikke at være bleven bemærket, end ikke
af C. Molbech, der dog omtaler Haandskriftet udførligt i Noten Side 39
i Henrik Harpestrengs danske Lægebog, Kjøbenhavn 1826.

Da jeg havde læst Afhandlingen, anstillede jeg nogle Under-
søgelser vedrørende Henricus de Dacias Identitet, og jeg fik derved
det Indtryk, at nævnte Forfatter og Henrik Harpestreng var samme
Person, uden at det dog lykkedes mig at føre det afgørende Bevis.
Begrundet paa en Rejse til Udlandet maatte Arbejdet lægges til Side
foreløbig, og under mit Fravær sendte jeg min Tydning af Haand-
skriftets Tekst til Dr. phil. Marius Kristensen, Askov, dels for at
faa Hjælp til de noget vanskeligere Steder, dels for at han, som
Udgiver af de nordiske Harpestrengstekster, kunde udtale sig om
Afhandlingen og dens Forfatter. Det blev da ogsaa Dr. Kristensen,
der fastslog Identiteten mellem Henricus de Dacia og Henrik Harpe-
streng.

Det vil altid have sin Vanskelighed, at foranstalte en Udgave af
et Manuskript, der kun kendes i en eneste Afskrift, navnlig naar
denne jævnlig indeholder Misforstaaelser og ikke er gjort med stor
Nøjagtighed. I det foreliggende Tilfælde har jeg valgt, netop paa
Grund af Afskriftens Mangelfuldhed, at lade Teksten tale for sig
translation:
While searching through the Royal Library's medical manuscripts, undertaken with the aim of, if possible, expanding knowledge of Danish physicians in the Middle Ages, I came across in Manuscript G. k. S. 1654, 4° a treatise, De simplicibus medicinis laxativis, written by a hitherto unknown author, Henricus Dacus or de Dacia. The manuscript in question is well known, not least on account of its containing a Macer text, but the treatise by Henricus Dacus appears until now not to have been noticed, not even by C. Molbech, who nevertheless discusses the manuscript in detail in a note on page 39 of Henrik Harpestreng's Danish Medical Book, Copenhagen 1826.

Having read the treatise, I conducted some investigations into the identity of Henricus de Dacia, and I formed the impression that the said author and Henrik Harpestreng were the same person, without however being able to produce conclusive proof. Due to a journey abroad, the work had to be set aside for the time being, and during my absence I sent my interpretation of the manuscript's text to Dr. phil. Marius Kristensen, Askov, partly to obtain help with the more difficult passages, and partly so that he, as editor of the Nordic Harpestreng texts, could express his opinion on the treatise and its author. It was indeed also Dr. Kristensen who established the identity between Henricus de Dacia and Henrik Harpestreng.

It will always present difficulties to produce an edition of a manuscript known only in a single copy, especially when that copy frequently contains misunderstandings and was not made with great precision. In the present case I have chosen, precisely on account of the copy's incompleteness, to let the text speak for itself

translation:
myself, and thus only exceptionally to correct errors and misunderstandings, just as I have not attempted to fill in missing words and sentences. This applies particularly to the Introduction, which in its present linguistic form is quite incomprehensible. The places in the text that seem to me entirely corrupted are marked with † placed before the relevant sentence, and punctuation has been added to ease comprehension. As for the frequently used sign ℥, I have read this as uncia. The sign is not found recorded in the commonly used palaeographic handbooks, and I have found justification for my reading in the fact that ½ pound was equal to 8 ounces, which is why one also finds in the section on fumus terræ: libra semis vel VIII ℥. I must however note that Avicenna (see the note sextum, p. 93) uses cotylus, where Henricus de Dacia has ℥, even though the texts otherwise agree. This need not involve any contradiction, since cotylus was most often equal to a libra, but its value was variable.
During the preparation of this work I have received help from many quarters. First and foremost I owe thanks to Dr. phil. Marius Kristensen for his repeatedly ready assistance. I also owe thanks to Professors J. L. Heiberg and Verner Dahlerup for advice and guidance, and particularly for the recommendations that gave me access to having this work published here in the country. A similar heartfelt thanks must also go to the Board of the Carlsberg Foundation, which granted the funds necessary for publication, and to Dr. V. Kuhr, who has been my tireless helper with linguistic difficulties.
A number of foreign scholars have conducted research on my behalf in libraries and archives in their home regions or have given me valuable assistance in other ways. I am thus indebted to Dr. Paul Dorveaux, librarian at the École supérieure de Pharmacie in Paris, Dr. Ernest Wickersheimer, librarian at the Académie de Médecine in Paris, and to Dr. Paul Delaunay in Le Mans. Furthermore, Dr. Garsonnier, archivist Jacques Soyer, and librarian A. Cagnieu have examined archives and libraries in Orléans on my behalf. Among German scholars, Hofrat, Dr. med. (h. c.) Max Höfler, of Bad Tölz near Munich, has repeatedly been of assistance to me. I ask them all to accept my warmest and most heartfelt thanks.

translation:
9

By dedicating my work to Dr. Paul Dorveaux, I have attempted to repay a small part of my debt to him. He was the first to forge the connection between France and the Danish physicians who occupy themselves with the history of medicine. Many Danes have over the years sought his help, but none have sought it in vain — least of all myself. The present work should therefore also serve as a token of the warm devotion I feel for my long-standing teacher and friend.

J. W. S. JOHNSSON.

February 1914.

text:
Den Afhandling, som her for første Gang skal udgives, bærer
Titlen: De simplicibus medicinis laxativis og har til Forfatter
en hidtil ukendt Henricus de Dacia, eller som han ogsaa benævnes
Henricus Dacus. Afhandlingen er optaget i et Samlebind, G. k. S.
1654, 4° i det kongelige Bibliotek i København, et Bind, der tillige
indeholder Skrifter af Johannes Parisiensis, Mattheus Platearius, Nico-
laus og Macer, foruden nogle mindre Stykker, blandt hvilke et bærer
Titlen Anbaleon. Henricus de Dacias Skrift er optaget f 104r—110r.

Et Spørgsmaal melder sig straks, hvem er denne Forfatter?
Drejer det sig om en hidtil ubekendt middelalderlig Forfatter fra
Danmark, eller skal Dacia her forstaas som hjemmehørende i et af
de tre nordiske Riger. Namnet Dacia betyder jo vel nok i Almin-
delighed Danmark, men bruges ogsaa i Betydning af Ordenspro-
vinsen, stammende fra Tiggermunkeordenernes Provinsialinddeling.
For Undersøgelsen vilde det da være af Betydning, om det kunde
være muligt at faa fastslaaet, indenfor hvilket Tidsrum Henricus de
Dacia havde levet, thi Dominikanerordenen kom Aar 1221 til Dan-
mark og Franciskanerne det paafølgende Aar, og Dacia vilde da
være fastslaaet som Danmark, hvis Henricus de Dacias Liv og Virken
faldt før disse Aar.

Nogen Forfatter af nævnte Navn synes ikke at være kendt af
nordiske Bibliografer. H. Schück¹ omtaler ingen Henricus Dacus,
Ellen Jørgensen² heller ikke. Manuskriptet giver selv ingen Oplys-

¹ H. Schück: Nordiska Medeltidsförfattere, en Artikel optaget i Bibliogra-
fiska och litteratur-historiska Anteckningar, Upsala 1896 p. 120.
² Ellen Jørgensen: Om nogle middelalderlige Forfattere, der nævnes som
hjemmehørende i „Dacia". Historisk Tidsskrift, 8 R III, 1911 p. 234.
Fr. Grøn har i et Foredrag i Kristiania Videnskabs-Selskab 24. April 1908
(offentliggjort i Norsk Magazin for Lægevidenskab 1908, No 10 under Titel: Nogle
translation:
The treatise that is here to be published for the first time bears the title: De simplicibus medicinis laxativis, and its author is a hitherto unknown Henricus de Dacia, also referred to as Henricus Dacus. The treatise is included in a miscellany, G. k. S. 1654, 4°, in the Royal Library in Copenhagen, a volume that also contains writings of Johannes Parisiensis, Mattheus Platearius, Nicolaus and Macer, along with some smaller pieces, among which one bears the title Anbaleon. Henricus de Dacia's text occupies folios 104r–110r.

A question immediately arises: who is this author? Is it a hitherto unknown medieval author from Denmark, or should Dacia here be understood as belonging to one of the three Nordic kingdoms? The name Dacia, of course, commonly means Denmark, but it is also used to denote the mendicant orders' provincial division. For the investigation it would be significant to determine within what period Henricus de Dacia lived, since the Dominican Order came to Denmark in the year 1221 and the Franciscans the following year, and Dacia would thus be confirmed as Denmark if Henricus de Dacia's life and work fell before those years.

No author of the mentioned name appears to be known to Nordic bibliographers. H. Schück¹ mentions no Henricus Dacus, and Ellen Jørgensen² does not either. The manuscript itself gives no information—

¹ H. Schück: Nordiska Medeltidsförfattere, an article included in Bibliografiska och litteratur-historiska Anteckningar, Uppsala 1896, p. 120.
² Ellen Jørgensen: Om nogle middelalderlige Forfattere, der nævnes som hjemmehørende i "Dacia". Historisk Tidsskrift, 8 R III, 1911, p. 234.
Fr. Grøn, in a lecture at the Kristiania Academy of Sciences on 24 April 1908 (published in Norsk Magazin for Lægevidenskab 1908, No. 10, under the title: Nogle

ning om, hvem den lille Traktats Forfatter er. Det er skrevet ned i Tiden omkring 1400—1450, samlet i Erfurt (f 184v: hec collecta sunt Erfordie) og kommet som Gave til Maria Klosteret i Segeberg (f 1r: liber domus sanctissime virginis marie et sancti Johannis ewangeliste in segeberghe per dominum luderum breme donatus).

En Henricus de Dacia er dog ikke ganske ukendt, idet der i M. s. fr. 1357, 2° (XVs) i Bibliothèque impériale (nu Nationalbiblioteket) i Paris findes omtalt en Henry de Danemarche. Noten om ham er optaget i Symon de Pharès: Receuil des plus célèbres astrologues et de quelques hommes doctes. Det paagældende Sted¹ lyder:

[f 119r] Maistre Henry de Danemarche excellent medecin à Orleans et grant astrologien en son tems fist de moult singulières predictions, iugements, pronosticacions et entre autre predict l'exil des Juifz de France et une des causes fust que au dict Orleans advint ainsi que ung prestre chantoit messe, après qu'il eust sacré le corps J. C. en le voulant prendre, apparut soubdainement tout sanglant, ce que sceut le roy Phelippe², qui y courust et le peuple de la ville et virent le sacrement en manière d'une piece de chair comme Inde[?] et dessus les corporaux apparoient gouttes des sang. Semblable miracle aparut au Vritour[?] de Vendosme et un autre en la cité d'Arras en un chastel que l'on appelle Sezamis, et furent environ l'an et le terme que le roy Philippes² fist paver la ville de Paris et clore de murs le bois de Vincennes l'an 1181.

Bemærkninger om Middelalderens medicinske Videnskab i Norden) omtalt nyere Membranfund i Norge, indeholdende Brudstykker af middelalderlige Forfatteres medicinske Skrifter. Han nævner Henrik Harpestreng, men ingen Henricus de Dacia. Det vilde forøvrigt ogsaa have været noget udenfor Foredragets Plan at omtale Personligheder udførligere, da dette væsentligst drejer sig om de middelalderlige Skolers Indflydelse paa norsk Lægekunst.
¹ Grev P. Riant: Et Bidrag til Vestigia Danorum extra Daniam i Chr. Bruun og O. Nielsen Danske Samlinger 1866—67 p. 270. Da Grev Riant i sin Kopi af Manuskriptet havde udeladt et Stykke (fra en maniere til Sezamis) har jeg forskaffet mig en Kopi af alt det paagældende gennem Bibliotekaren ved Académie de Médecine i Paris, Dr. Er. Wickersheimer. Jeg takker ham herved varmt, for hans, af danske ofte paakaldte, utrættelige Hjælpsomhed.
² Philippe II eller Philippe Auguste (1165—1223). Selv de korteste Biografier omtaler hans Virksomhed for Paris' Forskønnelse. Han byggede Slottet Vincennes.
translation:
11

concerning who the author of the little Treatise is. It was written down around 1400–1450, collected in Erfurt (f 184v: hec collecta sunt Erfordie) and donated as a gift to the Convent of Maria in Segeberg (f 1r: liber domus sanctissime virginis marie et sancti Johannis ewangeliste in segeberghe per dominum luderum breme donatus).

A Henricus de Dacia is, however, not entirely unknown, since in M. s. fr. 1357, 2° (15th century) in the Bibliothèque impériale (now the National Library) in Paris, a certain Henry de Danemarche is mentioned. The note about him is included in Symon de Pharès: Receuil des plus célèbres astrologues et de quelques hommes doctes. The relevant passage¹ reads:

[f 119r] Master Henry de Danemarche, excellent physician in Orleans and great astrologer of his time, made many singular predictions, judgments, and prognostications, and among other things predicted the exile of the Jews from France. One of the causes was that in the said Orleans it came to pass that a priest was singing mass, and after he had consecrated the body of J. C., when he wished to take it, it suddenly appeared all bloody, which King Philip² heard of, and he and the people of the city rushed there and saw the sacrament in the form of a piece of flesh like Inde[?], and upon the corporals there appeared drops of blood. A similar miracle appeared at Vritour[?] in Vendôme and another in the city of Arras in a castle called Sezamis, and these occurred around the time that King Philip² had the city of Paris paved and the Bois de Vincennes enclosed, in the year 1181.

Remarks on Medieval Medical Knowledge in the North mentioned newer parchment finds in Norway containing fragments of medieval authors' medical writings. He mentions Henrik Harpestreng, but no Henricus de Dacia. It would moreover have been somewhat outside the scope of the lecture to discuss personalities in greater detail, as it is primarily concerned with the influence of medieval schools on Norwegian medical practice.
¹ Count P. Riant: Et Bidrag til Vestigia Danorum extra Daniam in Chr. Bruun and O. Nielsen, Danske Samlinger 1866–67, p. 270. Since Count Riant had omitted a passage in his copy of the manuscript (from en maniere to Sezamis), I obtained a copy of the entire relevant section through the librarian of the Académie de Médecine in Paris, Dr. Er. Wickersheimer. I warmly thank him here for his tireless helpfulness, so often called upon by Danes.
² Philippe II or Philippe Auguste (1165–1223). Even the briefest biographies mention his work in beautifying Paris. He built the Castle of Vincennes.

Her er der ingen Tvivl om, at det drejer sig om en dansk Mand,
og at Henricus de Dacia ogsaa har været dansk og ikke nordisk,
tør vel fastslaas ved, at han i Traktatens Explicit nævnes som Hen-
ricus Dacus. Om Identiteten af de to Personligheder er det umu-
ligt at sige noget, om end det kunde være rimeligt at antage, at de
begge gik op i en tredje Person, den fra sine Urte-, Sten- og Læge-
bøger velkendte Henrik Harpestreng, hvis Dødsaar angives til 1244,
et Aar, der dog næppe er ganske sikkert¹. Nu er Forholdet imid-
lertid det, at Henrik Harpestrengs Liv og Levned er saa over-
ordentlig lidet kendte — man ved egentlig kun. at han var Medicus
et Canonicus Roschildensis, og at han var Kong Eriks (Plovpennings?)
Læge — at det i Øjeblikket er umuligt at finde Berøringspunkter i
det allerede meddelte. Vi skal nu se, om en Sammenligning mel-
lem de harpestrengske Skrifter og Henricus de Dacias Traktat kan
give noget Bidrag til Forstaaelse af denne og af dens Forfatters
Person. Hvorledes Forholdet til Henry de Danemarche er, vil da
senere blive at omtale.

¹ Aaret 1244 angives af mange Forfattere (Arild Huitfeld, J. Langebek, P. F.
Suhm). Det findes ogsaa hos Erik Pontoppidan, der anfører en Gravskrift, som
Harpestreng selv skal have skrevet.
translation:
12

There is no doubt here that we are dealing with a Danish man, and that Henricus de Dacia was also Danish and not Nordic, may well be established by the fact that in the Explicit of the Treatise he is referred to as Henricus Dacus. As for the identity of the two figures, it is impossible to say anything definitive, even though it might be reasonable to assume that both merged into a single third person, the well-known Henrik Harpestreng, familiar from his herbals, lapidaries, and medical books, whose year of death is given as 1244, a year that is, however, hardly entirely certain¹. The situation now is, however, that Henrik Harpestreng's life and career are so extraordinarily little known — one knows essentially only that he was Medicus et Canonicus Roschildensis, and that he was King Erik's (Plovpennings?) physician — that it is at present impossible to find points of connection with what has already been presented. We shall now see whether a comparison between the Harpestreng writings and Henricus de Dacia's Treatise can contribute to an understanding of both it and its author's identity. How the relationship to Henry de Danemarche stands will be discussed later.

¹ The year 1244 is given by many authors (Arild Huitfeld, J. Langebek, P. F. Suhm). It is also found in Erik Pontoppidan, who cites an epitaph that Harpestreng himself is said to have written.

Simples
translation:
Avicenna says in the book on simples that all medicines of simple laxative virtue have a certain preparatory purpose, and among physicians it is established that some are particularly suited to this use. The laxative simples, by their inherent quality, depend on repositories and, as stated by Italian and other authors, do not work without diligent attention to requirements; they produce a movement which purges certain medicines, and their laxative virtues, described in order, and set down as to which collection from the plants, and which compound medicines, and which collections of simples and their capacities are as follows:

Aloe — Of rhubarb — Of myrobalans
Agaric — Of dragagant — Of [various roots]
Armenian [clay] — Of quince — Of myrobalans [second variety]
[Various simples] — Of white ebulus — Of polypody
[Various simples] — Of black ebulus — Of rhubarb
Absinth — Of euphorbium — Of [herb]
Hellebore — Of hepatic [herb] — Of fumitory
Bdellium — Of gula — Of nettle
Centaury — Of fumitory — Of senna
Medella — Of quinates — Of turbith
Cassia fistula — Of hermodactyl — Of violet
Cucumber [wild] — Of fibula

Milk and the juice in a potion: it draws down and moves the stomach; it purifies and drives away vapors rising to the head, and drives them downward. For new uses, and for the treatment of idle animals and their conditions, suitable for hemorrhoidal remedy. Whoever needs the preparatory part should take it before: dragagant, or bdellium, or a little mastic, or milk. Before taking items of hepatic kind, it is praiseworthy and effective in loosening others, and when two [remedies] are joined, the administration is such that after five days the odors begin to diminish, and old colors and old virtues are restored; for virtue is best when it is drawn off with water or brine, and the strength is confirmed.

Take of these things half a dram, 4 parts in the compound, a medicine for the mouth; and 2 parts of small scruples; for simple drinking the lesser dose is 1 dram, the greater 2 drams, and alone it is slow to act, best taken before sleep for eating it brings benefit.

   In fevers it opens the bowels on both sides, and for the grosser humors it releases bile, clearing obstructions of the joints, helping those afflicted by numbness and mortification; if one is fasting on legumes and bathing, and better with white foods, the simple dose of these things is 1 dram, the lesser half, for another medicine of these things there is a purging effect.

   It is noted that against jaundice and melancholy this plant is sovereign against dropsy, pleurisy, certain fevers, palsy and arthritis. The dose of these things, middle measure: take 1 dram and a half dissolved in water of liquorice; the greater dose is 3, the lesser 2.

   One scruple, as the diet says, should take away yellowness and melancholy; the patient should attend carefully, not taking it too minutely, 4 times, to be ministered to for recovery. The middle dose is 3 drams, the greater 3 and a half, the lesser 2 and a half.

   For water gathered in the belly, purging the colon, take 2 drams more than sufficient; for the preparation of the decoction the dried root is best placed in boiling water so that the patient drinks it once a day at the fourth hour; not to exceed the middle dose; the drink should be taken through a tube of dried water, about one pound; it drives out the colon, makes the body thin from swelling, and cleanses of leprosy.

   Of asafoetida multiply as needed. For those constipated: for small bile passages, for hardness of the colon and for the gravel of the liver, and against mucus in the lungs, and for colic, it does not allow torpor to settle; its odor is of musk, and 4 parts suffice; against the evil vapors it absorbs bitterness, for four virtues it opens the opportunity for good function; it lasts, purifying the vessels and cleansing the belly, collecting mucus and binding it; against sweating take the juice; the dose is 2 drams, and its juice is the dose; the correction of the dose is 6 parts greater, the lesser 2; if one desires the best benefit:

   Of myrobolans: take dried myrobolans, and also of dried rose-hips, and also of gall-apples and aloe and acacia, which strengthens and dignifies the head; and also of the flower of [illegible] make a decoction for use.

GALEN says in his book on simple medicine that every simple laxative medicine has an attracting power upon its proper humors. It is therefore necessary for a physician to know what each simple laxative medicine properly purges; for from knowledge of these depends knowledge of compound medicines. ALOE is hot and dry in the second degree; by secondary action it draws out red bile and thick humors from the stomach, purges the brain of the same choleric and phlegmatic gross humors, and prevents vapors from rising from the stomach to the head, and therefore purges humors in the optic nerve and between the coats of the eye where they have gathered, and opens the mouths of hemorrhoids. Whoever therefore suffers from hemorrhoids needs to take it; let him take it with tragacanth or with a little bdellium or mastic. There are three species of aloe. By hepatic aloe we understand the following: it is more praiseworthy and more useful for loosening than the other two; it has a radiance like that of yellow gum, a more pleasant odor than the other species, breaks easily, is of a color resembling liver; old aloe is of little virtue, but fresh aloe is of more perfect virtue, whose use is most opportune if it is washed in water or simple goat's whey. Its medium dose is one drachma, and in compound medicines 3 scruples and 2 quarter-scruples; when taken by itself, the lesser dose is 5 I, the greater dose 5 III; its action is slow, and therefore one should not rush to eat after taking it.

AGARIC is hot and dry, hot in the second degree, dry in the third; it loosens both bile and thick phlegm, is moderate in its action, draws from the remote parts of the body...

ABSINTHIUM (wormwood) is hot and dry, yet it comes in many varieties; the best and most praiseworthy is of saffron color, having a soft down like the feathers of newly hatched pigeons, with a pleasant smell like that of hepatic aloe, and it has nodes in it. Its taste is strongly bitter with a certain astringency. It has the particular virtue of opening obstructions; it cures jaundice, cleanses the blood in the veins, purges red and black bile, cleanses the stomach of all unnatural bile; it draws together a loosened stomach, and powerfully purges black bile when compounded with epithyme, if its juice is taken. The dose is 3 drams; if a decoction of it is taken, the dose is 6 drams; the greater dose is four scruples, either somewhat less or somewhat more.

BELLIRICI have a cold and dry virtue; their actions are similar to those of citrine myrobalans. But they are of weaker action, and when used together with oak galls, henna, and vinegar, they strongly blacken the hair.

BDELLIUM is hot and moist; it has the virtue of loosening phlegm when drunk; the simple dose is 2 drams; when given with honey-water, half an exagium given with Indian, belleric, or kabuli myrobalans is beneficial for hemorrhoids and joint ailments located in the anus. Bdellium when hot and dry has the virtue of loosening phlegm.

CENTAUREA (centaury) is hot and dry; the finer variety is better; it purges red bile and viscous mixed phlegm, and is beneficial for joint pain, sciatica, and colic. Its juice is not drunk but used by physicians as a decoction. Its dose is

THE PITH OF THE GARDEN CROCUS is hot and dry, purges phlegm, treats dropsy, which I have proven, and benefits those suffering from colic. Its dose is 5 scruples V with a little oregano or Indian salt.

CASSIA FISTULA is hot and moist, purges by lubricating and drawing out, loosens gently, purges bile, expels hardened matter together with a little turbith, and relieves the pain of colic in the patient; yet without any other medicine it draws out gross humors, just as turbith does, and we say that turbith given together with cassia fistula draws out phlegmatic humors which, given alone, it is not sufficient to expel. Cassia fistula given with tamarinds expels bile; given with the juice of nightshade or the juice of fresh coriander it is beneficial in tertian fevers, and used as a gargle it dissolves an abscess of the throat. Cassia fistula is better when it is in the pod, and better still when the pod is thick and strong, which is the opposite of almonds.

The bitterness is lesser, the sharpness greater; they loosen thick and viscous phlegm, also black bile, and citrine bile, the water of dropsical patients; they benefit those suffering from phlegmatic conditions and from migraine, paralytics and those with colic. They are very strong. They should therefore be mixed with cassia fistula or with Aloe. Of these, however, they are better when collected at the setting of the Pleiades. If it is asked why we say that this [!] is the time of their completion — because those of them that are citrine in color are better, their juice is better in taste and substance, and the juice should not be expressed except by the strength of the hands or feet, and therefore take care not to grind them themselves. But if you wish to preserve it, pour off the clear water; keep the juice that appears after the residue until it thickens, so that you can make troches; make them and keep them for two parts of the year in their full strength, and after that their virtue diminishes. The dose taken by mouth is one half-scruple. If you wish to moderate its strength, add a little gum of the elders, or gum arabic, and a little wheat starch.

COLOQUINTIDA is hot and dry in the second degree; its pulp purges phlegm from the brain and the optic nerve and from the stomach, and prevents phlegmatic vapors from rising, and draws phlegm from the deep parts of the body. It is most praiseworthy when collected of saffron color at the setting of the Pleiades, for then it is perfect and complete. When incomplete it causes vomiting, dejection, sadness, disturbance, anxiety, and failure of breath, if it is given carelessly. And at times the medicine should be used with caution in great heat; moreover, the fat of the coloquintida outside its rind loses its strength within three months. It should therefore be kept safe, and since the flesh is rarely collected, we no longer recommend it; rather, let its harshness be tempered with a little gum arabic. Its average dose is two and a half scruples with gum arabic, and one and a half scruples without gum.

Similiter rectifi-catur cum Aloe et mirobolis et succo citoniorum et aqua decoctioni eorum, et quando citonia ponitur in confec-tionibus cum scamonea ipsa est velocioris operacionis et minoris malicie. Ex citoniis fiat quasi electuarium et apponatur in ea; dosis autem simplicis est 5 tertia pars cum frangentibus eius virtutem uel cum coquitur dosis est ℈ semis et grana X, maior dosis est ℈ I.

EPITHIMUM calidum est et siccum in principio tercii, eius est proprietas purgare coleram nigram habentibus et coleram rubeam superflue, non convenit immo nocet, probatum enim est quod facit eis turba-cionem et subuersionem, utile est desipientibus ex colera rubea nigra conbusta et naturali. Valet enim senibus et grandeuis, mundificat enim corpora eorum de melan-cholia. Epithimum laudabilius est cujus color in rubo-rem vergit et est fortis odoris; potus eius simplicis dosis est 5 II et semis, minor 5 II, maior 5 III; dedoctionis eius dosis 5 VII, minor 5 V, maior 5 IX, et quando vis vti epithimo simplici coqve aquam, et ferventem depone ab igne donec tepescat, tunc tritum epithimum adde et move
translation:
DIAGRIDIUM, that is scammony, is hot and dry in the third degree; it is most praiseworthy when fresh, tending toward a clear warmth, white with a clean, fine, glaucous surface, easily broken; such is found in Antioch. It purges red bile and its varieties, such as the citrine, green, leek-green, and rust-colored, as well as the phlegmatic humors with which it is mixed in the body. It purges with strong virtue, but because it tends to cause disturbance, cramping, and excoriation of the intestines, it must not be used except with caution. Its violence is broken by cooking it in the capsules of quince seeds. It is likewise corrected with Aloe and myrobalans and the juice of quinces and their decoction water, and when quince is placed in preparations with scammony itself, it is of faster action and less harmful. From quinces let a kind of electuary be made and the scammony placed in it. The simple dose is one-third of a dram, together with things that temper its virtue, or when it is cooked the dose is half a scruple and ten grains; the larger dose is one scruple.

EPITHYMUM is hot and dry at the beginning of the third degree. Its property is to purge black bile; for those who have an excess of red bile it is not suitable, indeed it is harmful, for it is proven that it causes them disturbance and upheaval. It is useful for those suffering from red bile, burnt black bile, and natural black bile. It is beneficial for the elderly and the aged, for it cleanses their bodies of melancholy. Epithymum is most praiseworthy when its color tends toward red and it has a strong odor. The simple drinking dose is 2 drams and a half, the lesser dose 2 drams, the greater 3 drams; the decoction dose is 7 drams, the lesser 5 drams, the greater 9 drams. And when you wish to use simple epithymum, boil water and remove it from the fire until it cools somewhat, then add the ground epithymum and stir.

ELLEBORUS ALBUS calidus et siccus in III; lau-

huius est proprietas flegma purgare grossum et magis
per vomitum quam per inferius sicud dicemus in se-

ELLEBORUS NIGER calidus et siccus in III; pro-
prium est illi laxare coleram rubeam et nigram.
Laudabilior est novus et niger bene qui mediocris inter
subtilem et grossam substantiam desipientie prodest ex
melancolia. Delet morpheas nigras cum ungentis, pro-

nigra; potus eius simplicis [dosis] est II 9, minor 9 se-

et rectificatur eius virtus per ipsum, et si non habemus
epithimum fiat cum decoctione satureie una tercia scru-

horum duorum simul ana.
translation:
24

Mix well and offer the mixture to be drunk. But if you wish to give a decoction together with other herbs, first cook the other herbs thoroughly and strain them, then add epithymum and leave it there until the strained liquid cools, and give it to drink. If you wish to give epithymum in its own substance together with a laxative decoction, cook the laxatives and afterwards strain the strained liquid, allow it to cool somewhat, then add 2 drams or 1 dram and a half of epithymum, mix it, and give it to drink. And it should be known that epithymum does not need any correction from another medicine; on the contrary, it corrects other medicines itself.


ELLEBORUS ALBUS is hot and dry in the third degree. The more praiseworthy kind is whiter and more uniform in texture. Its property is to purge thick phlegm, and more by vomiting than from below, as we shall describe in what follows.


ELLEBORUS NIGER is hot and dry in the third degree. Its particular property is to purge red and black bile. The most praiseworthy kind is fresh and genuinely black, of a quality midway between fine and coarse in substance; it is beneficial for madness arising from melancholy. It removes dark skin blemishes when used as an ointment; it is beneficial in leprosy and elephantiasis and in all diseases arising from black bile. The simple dose to be drunk is 2 obols, the larger dose half a scruple. It should, however, be given together with a decoction of epithymum, and its potency is corrected by that; and if we do not have epithymum, let it be given with a decoction of savory, one third of a scruple, and it is proven that it is better given with a decoction of both of these together in equal parts.

facit turbacionem torcionem et obpressionem in ore sto-
translation:
EUPHORBIUM is hot and dry in the fourth degree, of sharp strength. It is better when new, bright and lemon-yellow, and of strong odor. Its property is to purge watery matter from those with white phlegm, and phlegm from the joints and veins. It is beneficial for migraines, paralytics, and those with sciatica; it is not given by itself, but is therefore administered together with other medicines. The dose is a middle one of nine grains, the lesser six, the greater truly fourteen; it should be ground but not too finely, and in this form it should not be drunk, because it causes sadness, agitation, upset of the mouth and stomach, compression, sweating and weakness. So that these side effects may be avoided, the prescribed quantity is observed and there is added to it a little gum arabic of a weight of four or three grains. All those of a warm constitution and those in whom bile and blood predominate should beware of Euphorbium.

EUPATORIUM is hot and dry; it purges black bile. Hence it treats quartan fevers and apostemes, melancholy of the intestines, quintan fevers, and chronic fevers much aggravated by phlegm, when used with a decoction of agrimony. The dose at that time is two scruples and a half; if its juice is drunk, a half exagium with oxymel, it cures a true and established quartan fever. But if its decoction is given by itself, it is effective against the aforementioned, though in that case its dose is two drams, the lesser three, the greater six.

ESULA is hot in the third degree, dry in the second; it has both sharpness and a biting quality. Better is that whose color tends toward red. It is light in weight. In substance [106 v] it is fine; when prepared together with leather it is of dark color, of coarse substance, difficult to break, thorny; it is most harmful because it causes agitation, twisting, and oppression in the mouth and sto-

translation:
machi. Esula praiseworthy dissolves yellow water, phlegm, and the thick moisture of the joints; it helps with colic arising from phlegm and greasiness, and also loosens black bile. It has a milky juice, but its milk has no usefulness for loosening. Whoever wishes to suppress the harmful quality of esula should steep it for a day and night in sweet milk, and change the milk three or four times per day and night — I say day and night because if it is left longer it loses its virtue, or becomes too weakened. Afterward it should be removed from the milk, dried in the shade, and then powdered. If you wish to give it on its own, give it with anise and fennel or with a decoction of them. If it is given against colic from flatulence or thick phlegm, add roasted cumin and oxymel. If you wish to cure dropsical leucophlegmatic patients or those with general swelling (anasarca), after the herb has been steeped in milk, dried, and powdered, infuse it in water of nightshade and of fennel-flower, in equal parts, for three days; then strain the liquid and dry it in the shade until you can make lozenges. But first add a little Indian salt, or turbit, or both, or myrobalan, or aloe with turbit or Indian salt; and if you add a small amount of all of them it causes no harm, and it drives out yellow water gently and with good and great effect. Make the lozenges of this weight: one scruple, and let it be given with water of fennel and oxymel. In the other aforesaid diseases the dose is two drams, the lesser dose is half a scruple, and the greater is two and a half drams.

FUMITORY is cold and dry in nature. It has a certain bitterness that carries heat away from the stomach, it loosens red bile and purges it from burnt superfluities; gently but effectively it helps with itching and scabies arising from poisonous and burnt humors in the flesh and skin, and with leprosy. If the juice is drunk in a measure of half a pound or eight ounces,

flegma de iuncturis vnde valet sciaticis et poda-

translation:

well strained and first lightly cooked, and it should be given when drunk with 5 scruples of sugar. But it should not be cooked too much nor left uncooked at all, but well strained, and it has greater effect when not cooked.

POMEGRANATES, fresh and green, should be skinned and ground in a stone mortar, then pressed by hand or cloth; from that liquid take half a pound and mix it with 6 ounces and 2 scruples of sugar. This medicine relieves red bile by compression, and is good for loosening the bowels, for red bile, for extinguishing feverish heat, and for relieving headache in fevers caused by excessive heat. The dose is 3 ounces with a decoction of violets and plums, or either of them.

HERMODACTYLS are hot in the third degree, dry in the second, and purge phlegm from the joints, which is why they are beneficial for sciatica and gout arising from phlegm. Those that are white both inside and outside and hard to break are more praiseworthy; their dose is 1 scruple and a half with sugar. If mixed with another medicine, the dose is half a dram, or a little more or less, according to what seems best to the wise physician for particular cases. It should be noted that Hippocrates, writing on epidemic diseases, says that hermodactyls are very harmful to the stomach, and prescribes that ginger or cumin and similar things be mixed with them, for these strengthen the stomach against the harm done by hermodactyls, yet they do not remove their laxative effect. I have heard, however, that in raven's fat there resides the virtue of hermodactyls without harm to the stomach in purging.

KEBULI frigidi et sicci sunt in II. Saporem habent acerbum parum, proprie laxant coleram nigram et flegma, maxime si in stomacho sint; magis enim pur-gant comprimendo quam attrahendo, laxant etiam cole-ram rubeam sed debilius quam citrinam; dosis eorum media est VI 5. Si prohicitur substantia minor 3 IIII, maior vero 5 VIII. Nec consulimus quod detur substantia eorum, licet solitum sit fieri. Sed non dantur nisi cum decoctione aliqua, tunc autem sic decoctio laxans cole-ram nigram uel flegma uel coleram rubeam.

MIRABOLANI citrini frigidi sunt et sicci in II, sed tamen minus omnibus alijs speciebus mirabola-norum amari sunt, laxant coleram rubeam constringendo et comprimendo; dantur cum decoctionibus sine sub-stantia 5 V, maior dosis est 5 VII minor 5 IIII. Sed si das cum aqua simplici, calida in aqua fricentur; dosis media est 5 VI. Si datur substantia eorum, dosis est 5 III uel IIII. Sed plus valet sine substantia.

MIRABOLANI INDI laxant coleram nigram, quibus est ponticitas maior quam kebulis, et est virtus indorum proxima virtuti kebulorum. Sed inde forcius operantur. Dantur quia sicut kebuli, minuatur dosis par-cum valde. Notandum quod plus valent ad purgandum stomachum quam ad laxandum, soluunt enim stomachum quomodo galla corio, quando dantur in tota substantia; ad laxandum valent, quando fricantur in aqua uel de-coctione proiecta substantia et apposita zuccara de mi-rabolanis emblicis. non est multum curandum per se, dantur tunc cum alijs mirabolanis.
translation:
28

KEBULI are cold and dry in the second degree. They have a slightly bitter taste; they properly purge black bile and phlegm, especially when these are in the stomach; for they purge more by compressing than by drawing out. They also purge red bile, but less effectively than yellow bile. Their standard dose is 6 drams. If the substance is withheld, the lesser dose is 4 scruples, and the greater is 8 drams. We do not recommend that their substance be given, even though this is customarily done. They should only be given with some decoction, and in that case the decoction purges black bile, phlegm, or red bile.

CITRINE MYROBALANS are cold and dry in the second degree, but they are less bitter than all other varieties of myrobalans. They purge red bile by constricting and compressing. They are given with decoctions without the substance; the larger dose is 7 drams, the smaller 4 drams. But if you give them with plain water, let them be rubbed in warm water; the standard dose is 6 drams. If their substance is given, the dose is 3 or 4 drams. But they work better without the substance.

INDIAN MYROBALANS purge black bile; they have greater astringency than kebuli, and their virtue is closest among Indian varieties to that of kebuli. But they act more powerfully. They are given in the same manner as kebuli, but the dose should be reduced considerably. It should be noted that they are more effective for purging the stomach than for loosening the bowels; for they bind the stomach as a gall binds leather, when given in their full substance. They are effective as a laxative when rubbed in water or when the substance is cast off in a decoction and sugar from emblic myrobalans is added. They are not much to be relied upon by themselves; they are then given together with other myrobalans.

translation:
POLIPODIUM is hot in the first degree, temperate in moisture and dryness; it loosens and draws out melancholy and salty phlegm, purging gently and without haste. It is better when fresh, having a thick stem whose surface tends toward redness, and when broken is found to be green. When it is given, it should be ground and administered with a decoction of epithymum against melancholy, or with a small oxymel of vinegar and sugar, and water. If it is given against salty phlegm, it is sometimes given with plain water; the dose is then 2 drams and a half, the lesser dose 2 drams, the greater 3 drams. If it is to be given with laxative decoctions, give one or two scruples at most, and because it purges slowly, delay the meal; its decoction with broth of cabbage or of an old rooster loosens a constipated bowel. Next follows rhubarb.

RHUBARB is hot and moist; it has a viscosity by which it purges red bile without discomfort. Let 3 drams be boiled briefly in water, and let half a pound of this water be given, or two parts of a pound, boiled briefly so that its virtue is not dissolved. If it is given with water in which cassia fistula has been dissolved, it works more powerfully. If it is given in a decoction of violets and plums, it works well, and thus the quantity of rhubarb can be reduced if manna and tamarind are added, and a smaller quantity will suffice. In these ways it also helps with colic arising from a hot cause; if it is mixed with those remedies it causes turbidity, and it benefits those suffering from choleric complaints; from phlegm it does not cause turbidity. It benefits those who have a hot liver, and it dissolves hot abscesses that are in the viscera and joints, if it is given together with cassia fistula.

Its dose is one exagium at the lesser measure, three scruples, and at the greater one exagium and a half; it is given because it works well with a little oximel, or with honey-water, and more water besides.

SENNA is warm and dry at the end of the first degree; it purges red and black bile from the deep tissues of the body. It is useful for those with joint disease, sciatica, and gout arising from red bile, both without phlegm and with phlegm. Rasis says that it purges black bile along with the aforementioned, for these two reasons. It is good against scabies, itching, leprosy, morphea, and similar conditions. Cook seven ounces of senna and four and a half ounces of raisins with two ounces of strained liquid; add two ounces of sweet almond oil, and let it be drunk — it is beneficial for those suffering from red bile and phlegm. If you add five ounces of epithyme, it is good for melancholics, and so on; there follows:

TURBIT is warm and dry in the third degree; it purges phlegm. The most praiseworthy kind is flat on the surface, moderate in thickness and thinness, grey-green on the outside, white on the inside,

translation:
31

easily broken, sharp in taste and pungent, and gummy. Fresh it is more potent, old it is worth little or nothing; old turbith is recognized by the perforation of many of its fibers on account of age. Sometimes good quality is found and does not need much correction, since its malice is small. Its dose with decoctions is 3 drams, from 3 drams up to 4 drams; its dose in simple form is 1 dram up to 1 dram and a half. If you wish to give turbith in simple form, scrape the bark until you reach the white part. But if you wish to add it to antidotes or electuaries, grind it carefully, sift it, and add it; if used with laxative medicines, then moderately, lest it adhere too strongly to the villi of the stomach, and anoint it with rose oil or almond oil.

VIOLET is cold in the third degree, moist in the second; it purges red bile and relaxes by drawing it out. When tasted, it has a sharp edge and a sting almost like turbith, whence it purges but little; turbith is better, of purple color and pleasantly aromatic. If you wish to purge moderately, boil 6 ounces in 1 pound of water, strain to half and give it to drink thus; it loosens and purges bile in fevers and without fevers. If you wish to purge more strongly, add to the said decoction half a scruple of scammony, and if you wish to purge bile and phlegm, add 1 scruple and a half of turbith, and so forth.

NOTE that every medicine, whether strong or weak, should be given in a larger dose in a cold region than in a warm one. Whoever wishes to administer a laxative medicine must take many particular factors into account. A strong laxative medicine is not suitable for children, nor for the elderly, nor for the weak, nor in excessive heat, nor in excessive cold unless compelled; and if compelled, the air in the place where the medicine is given should be arranged so as to preserve—

Item commedat pontica, ut docet G[alienus]. Et si me-

et extrahe sanguinem, ne humores agregentur ad locum
unum. Item si times de malicia medicine, fac ut vomatur,
[108 v] uel da teriacam si est sine febre. Ad illud valet || omnis
res que frangit acumen medicine glutinacione uel unc-
tuositate uel lenificatione, in qua est dulcedo et suavitas.
Item non dormiat post medicinam, nisi cum velis re-
stringere. Item non exhibeas cibum ante perfectam pur-
gationem supra medicinam, nisi timeas defectum uel ut
stomachus fuerit valde calidus ad quem currit colera
uelociter, parum panis infusi in vino super medicinam
antequam medicina incipiat solucionem, uel si debilis
sit stomachus et calidus, ante medicinam humectetur et
confortetur cum aqua ordei vel succo malorum grana-

machus, sumat medicinam ieiunus. Sed tunc caven-
dum ne inveniat medicina stomachum omnino vacuum
translation:
32

...is better done in spring and autumn, as Hippocrates attests; for treatment at any time, the strong medicine must be properly prepared. Before the matter is administered, let it be digested and the passages lubricated — three things which Hippocrates indicates when he says: Bodies that you wish to purge must first be made fluid. Likewise, do not give two medicines at the same time, of which one acts quickly and the other slowly, as Galen attests in his commentary on the book Periconoxoon nosematon. If a good medicine does not work at the appointed hour — which happens either because of narrowness of the channels, or obstruction, or the crudeness of the matter — place upon the belly wool that has been washed and boiled in oil. If it does not loosen in this way and you are concerned, apply a clyster. If you are not concerned and the patient feels dizziness and suffers stinging pains in the stomach and hiccups, give 3 drams of mastic with warm water. Let him also eat bitter foods, as Galen teaches. And if the medicine has not worked after two or three days, open a vein and draw blood, lest the humors gather in one place. Also, if you fear the medicine is harmful, cause vomiting, [108 v] or give theriac if there is no fever. For all this it is helpful that everything which blunts the sharpness of the medicine does so through a binding quality, or unctuousness, or softening, in which there is sweetness and mildness. Also, the patient should not sleep after taking the medicine, unless you wish to restrain it. And do not give food before the medicine has fully purged, unless you fear weakness, or if the stomach is very hot and bile runs through it quickly — then give a little bread soaked in wine before the medicine begins to work, or if the stomach is weak and hot, let it be moistened and strengthened before the medicine with barley water or the juice of pomegranates or some other subtle and nourishing moist food. If the stomach is strong, let the patient take the medicine fasting. But then care must be taken that the medicine does not find the stomach completely empty.

But giving syrup on its own risks causing excoriation, unless it has been three or four days since, because then the belly is strong. If you fear excoriation and dysentery after a laxative medicine, give Armenian bole with the juice of pomegranates; or let the one who has taken the medicine bathe on the second day, so that whatever remains of the medicine may be evacuated through the bath, and if he takes pleasure in the bath, that is a good sign and he may remain longer. Let him drink no other broth before the medicine has fully worked its virtue, and this I say if the patient is strong, or if the medicine begins to make the liver ache — let him drink warm water; the same should be done if the liver aches after phlebotomy. Likewise, one who loosens the bowels in winter should keep to the south wind. But in summer to the north wind, or as Bartholomeus says, the physician should beware of giving medicine unless the moon is in Libra, or in Pisces, or in Scorpio. Likewise, a sign for knowing when the purging is sufficient is great thirst together with excess of what has been drawn out. Such thirst at times is not a sign of complete purging, and it does not arise from the quantity of the loosening, but from the condition of the mouth of the stomach — as when it is hot and dry — or from the medicine itself being purgative and warm, or because the humor to be purged is hot and dry, as with choler. Heat however loosens the belly: give ground nasturtium seeds or mastic, 3 drams twisted together, and give with mucilage of parsley or seeds of cucumber or a fomentation of wheat made from fine flour. If he suffers hiccups, give wine to drink, and sprinkle rose water over his face.

EMETIC medicine agrees with laxative medicines in the attraction of humors from the farthest parts of the body, but differs in evacuation and in the force of attracting humors, since the property of laxative medicines is to draw humors downward and discharge them into the bowel. The property of those that cause vomiting is to draw humors upward through the gullet and the mouth. They differ in their power of attraction, because laxatives draw more slowly and gently, emetics more quickly; thus emetics are of stronger virtue, laxatives of weaker; medicines causing vomiting attract from the extremities with force and by cutting through the hu-

The symptoms that arise from vomiting are: tension under the hypochondria, pain in the stomach, hiccups, loss of voice, stupor, and bleeding. Place a cloth soaked in oil of a decoction of rue on the extremities and over the abdomen; honey already given with warm water also helps. For the fifth complaint, strain the aforementioned oil and drip it into the ears of the patient and make him sleep. For the sixth, give him milk with wine, four and a half ounces of each, for it binds the blood and soothes the constitution. But if you wish to prevent the blood from congealing in the stomach and in the chest, give a syrup of vinegar with honey, etc.

Since we have heard of the virtues of simple laxative and emetic medicines, and the doses when they are given alone and when combined with others, and the rules for governing those taking laxative medicine and emetic medicine, it follows in order that we set down rules for the selection of these medicines and of all others, and for their gathering and preservation. But because we cannot choose well and usefully unless the way of selection is known, it is clear that the way must first be learned. This way consists of the substance of a medicine, its smell, taste, and color. Consider what substance the medicine you seek ought to have, what smell, what taste, what color. If you find a medicine that has all of these in the most perfect degree within its kind, it is to be chosen as the best. If a medicine is deficient in all of these qualities that it ought to have, it is the worst and is to be rejected. But if you find that it has some of the four aforementioned qualities and not others, that medicine will be intermediate between the best and worst of its kind. Hence it is that sugar is praised when it is very white and very sweet, with no substance of smell that is coarser than somewhat refined. The rose is praised when it is

well red, of aromatic odor, of pontic taste, of fine rather than coarse substance. The violet is praised, which is of purple color, of fine substance, of aromatic odor, somewhat sharp in taste, resembling these. It must be understood that all others, whether they be laxative or emetic or maturative or fortifying or possessing any other virtues whatsoever, etc.

[Marginal note. Foliage, root, seed, branch, flower, [110r] and gum and fruit collected for medicine in the best weather are better than those collected in rainy weather. And wild plants are stronger than domesticated ones. Mountain plants are stronger than other woodland plants of this kind.]

Medicinal plants that grow from the earth should be gathered when they have reached the peak of their perfection. The time of perfect ripeness for each is that in which the natural heat, aided by the external heat of the air, overcomes all excess or diminishment of the grain, at which time the substance, taste, smell, and color are at the height of their completion. Flowers, therefore, are gathered in spring, at the end of spring on the branch. Most seeds at the beginning of summer, fruits in the middle and end of it. Roots at the end of autumn, and the roots of each plant that grows from the earth should be gathered when its leaves have fully fallen. But this rule does not apply equally to all cases. Likewise, all things that grow from the earth should be gathered when the north wind is blowing, or because it rarely happens that plants at the time of collection are free from excess moisture, and once that is gone, more or less, it is necessary to dry them in the shade, or the time of drying and the time of storing should be clear and fair.

translation:
38

When you have thus gathered and dried them so that no moisture remains, it is necessary to protect them from spoilage. Aromatics should be stored together, foul-smelling substances together, poisonous ones together and separately, hot ones together, and cold ones together; understand the same regarding dry and moist substances, so that the potency of one does not corrupt the potency of another. All coagulated substances should be kept in chests whose wood is of white poplar; they should be of aspen or ash or beech or oak and similar woods that are not of strong odor or taste or otherwise of poor quality. Ambergris, musk, and other medicines of pleasant odor should be stored in silver, crystal, or glass vessels, and the mouths of the vessels should be stoppered. Moist medicines such as eye or ear salves should be kept in bronze vessels; marrow, fats, and lard should be kept in lead vessels. Oils, however, are best kept in glass vessels, and waters in earthenware or glass vessels. These are the complete matters which from the beginning we proposed to set in order.
Here ends the dispensatory of Master Henrik the Dane.

text:
Ved Gennemlæsningen viser den foreliggende Traktat sig at til-
høre de Arbejder, der oprindelig var udgaaede fra den Salerni-
tanske Skole. Det er derfor heller ikke for intet, at den er optaget
i et Bind, der næsten kun indeholder Skrifter af Forfattere, stam-
mende fra dette Sted. En Sammenligning med de Harpestrengske
Skrifter viser to store Hovedforskelligheder. Først og fremmest er
det foreliggende Skrift skrevet paa Latin i Modsætning til alle de
Harpestrengske, der kun er kendte i Redaktioner i nordiske Sprog,
dernæst er Traktaten et videnskabeligt Arbejde, der efter hele sin
Form henvender sig til et sagkyndigt Publikum, ja, maaske til en
Tilhørerskare, hvilket enkelte Udtryk kunde tyde paa. De Harpe-
strengske Skrifter vender sig derimod til det læge Folk, alene
Sproget viser det, og i hvilken Grad de er blevne Lægmands
Eje, behøver vel neppe at omtales her. Er Henricus Dacus = Henrik
Harpestreng, vilde vi da for første Gang staa overfor et viden-
skabeligt Arbejde af Middelalderens berømteste danske Læge. Og
at de to Personer er identiske, bevises ved, at Afhandlingen om de
laxative Midler indeholder Originalteksten til det 81. Afsnit af Urte-
bogen, et Stykke, til hvilket ingen Forfatter eller rettere intet For-
billede hidtil var kendt, og som i den danske Tekstredaktion delvis
er ordret oversat fra den latinske, men som rigtignok samtidig er
blevet saa væsentligt ændret og forkortet, at det er gaaet ud over
Forstaaelsen, der sine Steder er ret vanskelig. Kapitlet gør jo ogsaa
som Helhed et noget spredt og sammenstykket Indtryk. En Sam-
menligning af de paagældende Steder vil vise, hvor nær de to Tekster
følges ad. Jeg aftrykker her den danske Tekst og desuden de paa-
gældende Steder af Henricus Dacus' Afhandling, idet Afsnittet i sin
Helhed er offentliggjort i den samlede Tekst (pag. 31—34).
translation: Upon reading through it, the present treatise reveals itself as belonging to the works that originally emanated from the Salernitan School. It is therefore no accident that it has been included in a volume containing almost exclusively writings by authors originating from that place. A comparison with the Harpestreng writings reveals two major differences. First and foremost, the present work is written in Latin, in contrast to all the Harpestreng writings, which are known only in versions in the Nordic languages; secondly, the treatise is a scholarly work that, by its very form, addresses a learned audience, indeed perhaps a body of listeners, as certain expressions suggest. The Harpestreng writings, by contrast, address the common people, and the language alone demonstrates this, while the degree to which they have become the property of laymen hardly needs to be mentioned here. If Henricus Dacus is the same person as Henrik Harpestreng, we would then be standing for the first time before a scholarly work by the most celebrated Danish physician of the Middle Ages. And that the two persons are identical is proven by the fact that the treatise on laxative remedies contains the original text for the 81st section of the Herb Book — a passage for which no author, or rather no source, had previously been known, and which in the Danish textual version is in part translated word for word from the Latin, but which, it must be admitted, has at the same time been so substantially altered and abbreviated that comprehension, which in certain places is quite difficult, has suffered as a result. As a whole, the chapter also gives a somewhat scattered and patchwork impression. A comparison of the relevant passages will show how closely the two texts follow one another. I reprint here the Danish text and also the relevant passages from Henricus Dacus' treatise, since the section in its entirety has been published in the collected text (pp. 31–34).

HENRIK HARPESTRENG.
Whoever wishes to take a laxative medicine must know this: that no strong medicine may be given to children, nor to very old people, nor to others who are sick, nor should medicine be taken or given when there is great heat, nor in great cold. One should not take two medicines in one day. When a laxative medicine has been taken and one has obtained loosening of the bowels, food should not be taken before the medicine has fully completed its work. If he takes food before that, he may expect to get a bad sickness. He who has drunk medicine may bathe on the following day, so that what remains of the medicine may be expelled through the bath. If he greatly desires a bath, that is a good sign, and if he tolerates great heat, then he may go out. After the loosening let him drink a broth of barley. If a man feels pain in the liver after the medicine, or after bloodletting, then let him drink warm water. When one who has taken medicine for loosening of the bowels sometimes gets vomiting and no loosening, and this happens because of that weakness that the stomach has — often, and the one who drinks a vomiting draught gets loosening and no vomiting, that is because the stomach is strong. Whoever wishes to...

HENRICUS DACUS.
Whoever wishes to administer a laxative medicine must consider many particular things. A strong laxative medicine is not suitable for children, nor for the elderly, nor for the weak, nor in excessive heat, nor in excessive cold. One should not give two medicines at the same time. Item: do not offer food before the medicine has completed its full purging, unless you fear a deficiency. He who drinks the medicine should bathe on the second day, so that whatever of the medicine remains may be expelled through the bath; and if he takes pleasure in the bath, that is a good sign and he may remain longer. If he suffers after the heating, let him leave immediately. Or after the loosening let him drink barley water. If from the medicine the liver begins to ache, let him drink warm water; do the same if the liver aches after bloodletting. Item: he who loosens the bowels in winter...

In winter he should seek the south wind. In summer one should seek the north wind for healing. Note that when illness involves looseness and it has become very great thirst, and when it has come to pass, if he wishes thereafter that the illness has been fully completed within, then he shall drink wine, and rose water shall be sprinkled on his face.

[Latin column:] It serves the south wind. In summer, however, the north wind... [several lines of dots indicating gaps in the text] Item: a sign of knowing when the purging is sufficient is great thirst... [more gaps] ...he should drink wine and sprinkle rose water upon the face.

As can be seen, the two texts follow one another closely, so closely indeed that there can be little doubt that the Danish text is a translation of the Latin. Only at one single place (When illness of looseness is taken up, and a man has received relief, food shall not then be taken, etc.) can discussion arise as to from which point in the Latin text the translation was made. The idea about the dangerous consequences of eating before the laxative medicine has taken effect is also present at pages 32–33 in the sentences: But then one must take care that the medicine does not find the stomach completely empty of food, because the stomach may be greedy for medicine, and after the medicine begins to purge you must not eat before its power has rested, because if you give food afterwards, a future fever is to be feared. This, however, has no bearing on the internal relationship between the two texts, and it can well be established that Henricus Dacus or de Dacia is the same person as Henrik Harpestreng.

In the form in which the herbal books exist, they contain only one Arabic drug, the somewhat doubtful Zedoar¹. In the treatise published here the situation is different. Here a series is included (Cassia, Mirabolanus, Rhabarbarum, Sennes, Turbith etc.)²,

translation:

And the commentary presented here will also show to what degree the treatise is built not only on Rhazes, mentioned by Henricus de Dacia, who is but little used, but equally and most significantly on Avicenna and several other Arabic authors (Kopho).

That Rhazes (850–923 (932)) is explicitly named in the text is perhaps due to the fact that he marks the introduction and beginning of "the Arabic art of medicine." He genuinely renewed medical study in several ways, not least by attempting to bring chemistry into the service of medical science.

After this, it seems as though "De simplicibus medicinis laxativis" belongs to a somewhat later period than the Herb Books. Yet this is by no means certain. It is hardly likely that Harpestreng, when writing the Herb Books, would have included drugs that the common man in every case would have found difficult to obtain, and which had perhaps only recently gained wider recognition in learned medical science. It is more reasonable to suppose that he deliberately omitted such things and only mentioned them in treatises addressed to a different stratum of the population than the layman. It is also quite characteristic that the texts converge precisely at the point where the concern was to give rules for the sick — rules that could be used by all and sundry.

Modestino del Gaizo, who according to De Renzi, Daremberg, and Henschel has taken the Salerno school as his subject of investigation¹, states that it passed through five different periods in its development. The first he calls the cenobitical, and it falls before the year 1000. The next period extends a hundred and fifty years further in time, during which ancient medicine experienced its rebirth. The third, the 12th century, is characterized by the popular and hygienic nature of the medical art, while the surgical schools were established in the fourth period, the 13th century. The period of decline lasted from the fourteenth century until 1811.

To determine the time boundary of the treatise under consideration here, one may look to the Salernitan names that Henricus Dacus mentions. These are Bartholomeus, Nicolaus, and Constantin. In addition, partly

The sources are namely Avicenna and Kopho the younger. Of Bartholomeus' life nothing further is known beyond the fact that he was a pupil of Constantinus Africanus. His year of death is therefore not known. Nicolaus, the celebrated author of the Antidotarium, lived around 1140, and Constantin was born in Carthage around 1018 and died in 1087 or somewhat later. Avicenna died in 1037, while Kopho the younger wrote his works in the years 1085–1100. After this, "De simplicicus medicinis laxativis" must have been written after c. 1150 and therefore most closely aligns with the third section of the Salernitan school, which the nature of the treatise also indicates.

It remains to investigate whether "Maistre Henry de Danemarche" could be identical with Henrik Harpestreng. It cannot be proven, but there is some likelihood of it, or at least it is not impossible. From very ancient times there has been a lively connection between France and Denmark. La Porte du Theil¹, who devoted particular attention to relations between the two countries in the 12th century, and who gives extensive account of their rich political and scholarly intercourse, even asserts that the connection with France was, for Denmark's part, more lively than with any other country. For the 13th–15th centuries, Er. Wickersheimer has provided some information², showing what esteem Danish physicians enjoyed in France. However, no Henricus Dacus is mentioned by these authors, nor is he found mentioned in Budinszky's³ list of Danes who studied at the University of Paris during the Middle Ages⁴. The account of "Maistre Henry de Danemarche" is localized to Orléans, which is yet further evidence of the great role that city played for Danish scholars. Elsewhere I have given an account—

position¹ of Danish physicians' periods of study and work in France, and my investigation yielded the result that of twenty-two Danish physicians who took their doctorate in France between 1500 and 1700, fourteen were doctors from Orléans (two of these also held degrees from Caen and Montpellier). This city was thus the preferred one, a circumstance that can hardly have arisen suddenly, but must have asserted itself in earlier periods, for which it will now be difficult to demonstrate in the case of physicians, since the biographical data for Danish medieval physicians are very incomplete. How much lies in the expression "à Orléans" is not easy to say; in context it means little more than that the person in question resided there for a shorter or longer period. More complete data are needed to determine whether Master Henrik studied there, or whether he possibly took his degree in Orléans.

To have this question answered, investigations must be conducted in the local archives. So far such a search has yielded no result. In the Departmental Archive for Loiret no document has been found in which any Henrik of Denmark is named, and the search in Orléans' municipal archive has likewise been in vain².

It would be quite natural to look for a Henry de Danemarche in Montpellier, but for the earliest period of that school no information whatsoever is available. It was founded around 1150, and the first document relating to it is dated January 1180³, a point in time when Henry de Danemarche was presumably already in Orléans.

i Rostock, senere drog til Erfurt og absolverede Magistergraden
der Aar 1425. Han blev Rektor for Universitetet sammesteds i
Vinteren 1434—35 og Doctor juris utriusque. Aar 1451 udnævntes
han til Biskop i Viborg. Der vides imidlertid intet om de Bøger,
translation:
45

Simon de Pharès's note establishes with certainty that the year 1181 was the time of the miracle that occurred, which must coincide with the period of Henry de Danemarche's stay in Orléans. If this Henry is indeed identical with Henrik Harpestreng, then the latter must have died as a very old man. Between the two years, 73 years have passed, and since the Danish scholars set out on their travels abroad while still quite young, Henrik Harpestreng must have reached an age of around ninety years, which admittedly could lie within the bounds of possibility. It can therefore certainly not be established that the two persons are identical.

When one considers the relationship between Harpestreng's Herbal and the present article, De simplicibus medicinis laxativis, the question arises whether Harpestreng first wrote his books in Latin and later partly used them for what one might call more popular writings. Whether this is the case, or whether his work as an author falls into two parts — a scholarly one, which unfortunately is still very little known, and a popular one, which long ago earned him a reputation throughout all of Scandinavia — is not known. These questions cannot be answered at present. The manuscript discussed here is the only one that has so far come to light under the name of Henrik Dacus, and despite much searching I have not succeeded in finding more. Such will surely come to light, however, as the great libraries' manuscript collections are registered and worked through.

In one respect the present manuscript is remarkable, namely in that it originates from Germany, from Erfurt. It would therefore be of interest to try to learn something about how it came to Denmark, but here again the search proves elusive, and one is left with possibilities. A connection between Denmark and Erfurt can be demonstrated in the period 1400–1450, which roughly corresponds to the manuscript's time of writing, in that Knud Mikkelsen, who was matriculated at Rostock in 1421, later went to Erfurt and took his Master's degree there in 1425. He became Rector of the University there in the winter of 1434–35 and Doctor juris utriusque. In 1451 he was appointed Bishop of Viborg. However, nothing is known about the books,

text:
